In what year was Hamish Harding born?
Hamish Harding: George Hamish Livingston Harding (24 June 1964 – 18 June 2023) was a British businessman, pilot and adventurer based in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
In what year did Aristotle die?
Aristotle (Ancient Greek: Ἀριστοτέλης, romanized: Aristotélēs; 384–322 BC) was an ancient Greek philosopher and polymath.
In what year was Phosphorus discovered?
Phosphorus is a chemical element; it has symbol P and atomic number 15.

Sukhoi Su-57: Komsomolsk-on-Amur Aircraft Production Association. The Sukhoi Su-57 (Russian: Сухой Су-57; NATO reporting name: Felon) is a twin-engine stealth multirole fighter aircraft developed by Sukhoi.
In which country did the Hawker Hurricane take place?
Hawker Hurricane: United Kingdom. The Air Ministry ordered Hawker's Interceptor Monoplane in late 1934, and the prototype Hurricane K5083 performed its maiden flight on 6 November 1935.
Who is credited with discovering Norma?

Norma (constellation): Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. Its name is Latin for normal, referring to a right angle, and is variously considered to represent a rule, a carpenter's square, a set square or a level.
Who is credited with discovering Aspartame?
Aspartame: James M. Schlatter. Aspartame is an artificial, non-saccharide sweetener commonly used as a sugar substitute in foods and beverages.
Who is credited with discovering Histamine?
Histamine: Henry Hallett Dale. Histamine or histamin is an organic nitrogenous compound found in mammals and many vegetables, fruits and food products.
About 5 million tonnes of acetic acid are produced annually largely to make this compound, most commonly in polymer form — what is it?
Acetate is a salt formed by the combination of acetic acid with a base (e.g. sodium hydroxide), an ester of acetic acid, or the anion CH3COO- found in solution.

Native to South America but cultivated in Europe since the 17th century for its fragrant oil, this flowering member of the verbena family is better known by a common name referencing a citrus fruit — what's its scientific name?
Aloysia citrodora is a species of flowering plant in the verbena family Verbenaceae, native to South America.
This scientific discipline bridges biology and sociology, studying human behavior, cultures, societies, and languages across time. What field is it?

Anthropology is the scientific study of humanity that crosses biology and sociology, concerned with human behavior, human biology, cultures, societies, and linguistics, in both the present and past, including archaic humans.

It's one of the oldest natural sciences, recruiting math, physics, and chemistry to explain everything that originates beyond Earth's atmosphere — from comets and quasars to the cosmic microwave background. What field is it?
Astronomy is a natural science that studies celestial objects and the phenomena that occur in the cosmos.
This perennial flowering plant species, native to Eurasia and growing up to four feet tall, includes cultivated varieties used for sugar, its edible root, and its edible leaves — what species is it?
Beta vulgaris (beet) is a species of flowering plant in the subfamily Betoideae of the family Amaranthaceae.
Members of this decapod infraorder tuck a tiny tail-like abdomen under a hard thorax and end their front legs in pincers — which true creatures are they?
Brachyura is an infraorder of decapod crustaceans comprising the true crabs.
This opportunistic yeast lives harmlessly in the gut and mouth of most healthy adults, but can turn pathogenic in immunocompromised people, causing a common fungal infection — what species is it?
Candida albicans is an opportunistic pathogenic yeast that is a common member of the human gut flora.
Famous for color-shifting camouflage and zygodactylous, pincer-like feet, which family of roughly 200 Old World lizard species is this?
Chameleon (family Chamaeleonidae) are a distinctive and highly specialized clade of Old World lizards with 200 species described as of June 2015.

Largely self-taught and grinding his own lenses from spare parts on a Kansas farm, this astronomer's homemade skills landed him at Lowell Observatory — where his 1930 survey turned up the first known body in the Kuiper belt; who was he?

Clyde Tombaugh (February 4, 1906 - January 17, 1997) was an American astronomer and telescope maker, best known for discovering Pluto in 1930, marking the first detection of what would eventually be recognized as the Kuiper belt.
Derived from Greek words meaning universe and study of, this scientific and philosophical field examines the nature of existence at the grandest scale — what is it called?
Cosmology (from Ancient Greek (cosmos) 'the universe, the world' and - (logia) 'study of') is the study of the nature of the universe, the cosmos.
This Asian canid stands apart from true dogs: a convex rather than concave skull, no third lower molar, and single-cusped upper molars — once it roamed into Europe. What is it?
Dhole (dohl; Cuon alpinus) is a canid native to South, East and Southeast Asia.
Which natural science examines how living things relate to their environment, spanning the individual, population, community, ecosystem, and biosphere levels?
Ecology (from Ancient Greek (okos) 'house' and - (-loga) 'study of') is the natural science of the relationships among living organisms and their environment.

This Austrian physicist devised a foundational equation for calculating a quantum system's wave function and coined the term 'quantum entanglement,' sharing the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with Paul Dirac — who is he?
Erwin Schrödinger (12 August 1887 - 4 January 1961), sometimes written as Schroedinger or Schrodinger, was an Austrian theoretical physicist who developed fundamental results in quantum theory.

This Arabic term describes the human interpretation and practice of Islamic religious law, expanded through jurists' scholarly reasoning and expressed in the rulings they issue on questions of faith. What is this field called?
Fiqh is the term for Islamic jurisprudence. Thus, whereas sharia is considered immutable and infallible by Muslims, fiqh is considered fallible and changeable.
Practitioners of this discipline monitor crustal motion, tides, and polar shifts to maintain accurate global positioning reference frames — what is this field called?
Geodesy (jee-) or geodetics is the science of measuring and representing the geometry, gravity, and spatial orientation of the Earth in temporally varying 3D space.
Endemic to Africa and among the oldest of the gallinaceous birds, this family branched off before New World quail evolutionarily — name the birds?
Guinea fowl are birds of the family Numididae in the order Galliformes.
Planted for land reclamation thanks to its nitrogen-fixing, erosion-resisting root system, this deciduous shrub genus's berries also show up in human and animal food products — what genus is it?
Hippophae is a genus of flowering plants in the family Elaeagnaceae.

Once diagnosed almost exclusively in women as a physical illness in the 19th century, this term for ungovernable emotional excess later became the focus of research by Freud and Charcot — what is this condition called?
Hysteria is a term used to mean ungovernable emotional excess and can refer to a temporary state of mind or emotion.

This American economist gave his name to a model for censored dependent variables — the 'tobit' — and advised the Council of Economic Advisers while championing government action to head off recessions. Who was he?

James Tobin (March 5, 1918 - March 11, 2002) was an American economist who served on the Council of Economic Advisers and consulted with the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, and taught at Yale University.
A founder of modern geometric analysis, this American mathematician won the 2019 Abel Prize for pioneering work in geometric PDEs and gauge theory — who is she?
Karen Uhlenbeck (born August 24, 1942) is an American mathematician and one of the founders of modern geometric analysis.

A Cornell-trained engineer and Atlanta factory superintendent, this man was wrongly convicted of a young employee's murder, then kidnapped from prison and lynched in a case now central to American antisemitism — who was he?

Leo Frank (April 17, 1884 - August 17, 1915) was an American lynching victim wrongly convicted of the murder of 13-year-old Mary Phagan, an employee in a factory in Atlanta, Georgia, where he was the superintendent.
Born in Winnipeg and trained at King's College London, this physicist and chemist joined the Manhattan Project in 1942 to conduct experiments with uranium — who is he?
Louis Slotin (1 December 1910 - 30 May 1946) was a Canadian physicist and chemist who took part in the Manhattan Project.
He helped uncover the Antarctic ozone hole and shared a 1995 Nobel for exposing the danger CFCs pose to the ozone layer — which Mexican chemist?
Mario Molina (19 March 1943 - 7 October 2020) was a Mexican physical chemist.
Connecting the diencephalon and cerebrum to the pons, this brainstem structure plays a role in vision, hearing, and staying alert -- what is it called?
Midbrain is the uppermost portion of the brainstem connecting the diencephalon and cerebrum with the pons.

Chemically known as bis(2-chloroethyl) sulfide, this organosulfur compound is a potent alkylating agent and carcinogen with no preventive antidote — protection relies entirely on covering the skin and airways. Name this notorious chemical warfare agent?
Mustard gas are names commonly used for the organosulfur chemical compound bis(2-chloroethyl) sulfide, which has the chemical structure S(CH2CH2Cl)2, as well as other species.
Element 102 honors the inventor of dynamite, and its short-lived isotope 255 — with a 3-minute half-life — is the one chemists actually prefer to work with. Which synthetic actinide is it?
Nobelium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol No and atomic number 102.
Dubbed the father of nuclear chemistry, he studied under Ernest Rutherford before helping identify the radioactive elements radium, thorium, and protactinium — who is he?
Otto Hahn (8 March 1879 - 28 July 1968) was a German chemist who was a pioneer in the field of radiochemistry.
Listed in the Dictionary of Fungi as containing over 300 species, this mold genus produces a compound that stops bacterial growth and also flavors certain cheeses — which genus?
Penicillium is a genus of ascomycetous fungi that is part of the mycobiome of many species and is of major importance in the natural environment, in food spoilage, and in food and drug production.
Equal to one-eighth of a gallon in both the imperial and US customary systems, this unit of volume is just over 20% larger in Britain than it is in America — name it?
Pint (symbol pt, sometimes abbreviated as p) is a unit of volume or capacity in both the imperial and United States customary measurement systems.
Originating on Gran Canaria and Tenerife, this large Spanish mastiff-type breed was traditionally used to guard property, herd livestock, and, legally until 1936, fight other dogs — what breed is it?
Presa Canario is a Spanish breed of large dog of mastiff or catch dog type.
It can form not just from rain but from mist, spray, or dew, and though we usually see an arc, it can actually be a full circle — what optical phenomenon is it?
Rainbow is an optical phenomenon caused by refraction, internal reflection and dispersion of light in water droplets resulting in a continuous spectrum of light appearing in the sky.
Named for its type genus, this plant family of nearly 4,800 species includes the trees and shrubs behind apples, pears, plums, cherries, and peaches — what family is it?
Rosaceae is a family of flowering plants that includes 4,828 known species in 91 genera.
This synthetic element, atomic number 106, is so fleeting that only a few atoms exist at a time and decay within minutes — and it's named for an American nuclear chemist; what is it?
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Sg and atomic number 106.
Doctors recommend covering your elbow rather than your hands to block this involuntary, explosive rush of air from spreading illness through the air. What is this reflex called?
Sneeze (also known as sternutation) is a semi-autonomous, convulsive expulsion of air from the lungs through the nose and mouth, usually caused by foreign particles irritating the nasal mucosa.
This muscular, hollow organ in the upper digestive tract handles the gastric phase of digestion, and gives us the medical prefix 'gastric' from its Ancient Greek name — name the organ?
Stomach is a muscular, hollow organ in the upper gastrointestinal tract of humans and many other animals, including several invertebrates.
Sporting beaded antennae and a pale, soft-bodied worker caste, these decaying-wood eaters belong to the order Isoptera and are really highly derived cockroaches — what are they?
Termite are a group of eusocial insects which consume a variety of decaying plant material, generally in the form of wood, leaf litter, and soil humus.

Caused by the parasite Toxoplasma gondii and often spread through undercooked meat or contact with infected cat feces, this disease can be especially dangerous to a developing baby if a woman is infected during pregnancy — what is it?
Toxoplasmosis is a parasitic disease caused by Toxoplasma gondii, an apicomplexan.
This type of blood vessel usually carries deoxygenated blood toward the heart — except in the pulmonary and fetal circulation, where it carries oxygen-rich blood instead — what is it?
Vein is a blood vessel in the circulatory system of humans and most other animals that carries blood towards the heart.
This noble gas, found in trace amounts in Earth's atmosphere, powers arc lamps, serves as a rare anesthetic, and was the first of its family coaxed into a genuine chemical compound — which element?
Xenon is a chemical element; it has symbol Xe and atomic number 54.
Known by the common name yarrow, this pungent, fernleaved plant in the daisy family is used in traditional medicine and as livestock feed — what is its scientific name?
Achillea millefolium: Species of plant. Achillea millefolium, commonly known as yarrow or common yarrow, is a flowering plant in the family Asteraceae.
A former IMF economist, this politician has served as President of Ivory Coast since 2010 after earlier stints as the country's prime minister in the early 1990s — who is he?
Alassane Ouattara: President of Ivory Coast since 2010. Ouattara became the president of the Rally of the Republicans (RDR), an Ivorian political party, in 1999.
Also known as shadbush, serviceberry, or juneberry, this rose-family shrub's berries inspired the name of a Canadian city — which genus?
Known in veterinary medicine as inappetence when it strikes cats, dogs, or cattle, which general medical term describes any loss of appetite — a symptom rather than a diagnosis in itself?
Anorexia (symptom): Loss of appetite. The symptom also occurs in non-human animals, such as cats, dogs, cattle, goats, and sheep.
Caused by excessive exposure to silver dust or compounds, this condition turns the skin a striking blue or blue-gray shade, especially in sun-exposed areas — what's it called?
Argyria: Medical condition. The most dramatic symptom of argyria is that the skin turns blue or blue-gray, and is usually most prominent in sun-exposed areas of the skin.
Evolving from a troubled twin-engine predecessor into a four-engine heavy bomber powered by Rolls-Royce Merlin engines, which British WWII aircraft became one of the RAF's most famous bombers?
Avro Lancaster: World War II British heavy bomber aircraft.
This common, noncancerous enlargement of a male gland can cause frequent urination and a weak stream; it isn't linked to poor hygiene, and there's no known cure. What's the condition?
Benign prostatic hyperplasia: Noncancerous increase in size of the prostate gland.
Believed to descend from hounds once kept at a Belgian abbey, this scent hound can follow a human trail days old and is a favorite of police tracking escaped prisoners — which breed is it?
Bloodhound: Dog breed used for tracking by scent.

This tropical tree's moderately ripe flesh, once cooked, is said to taste like a fresh-baked loaf with a potato-like flavor, and 18th-century navigators carried it in seedless form to the Caribbean — what is it?
Breadfruit: Edible fruit-bearing tree in family. Moraceae.
The fifth most abundant element in Earth's crust and a reactive alkaline earth metal, this element's name comes from the Latin word for 'lime' obtained by heating limestone — what is it?
Calcium: Chemical element with atomic number 20 (Ca)
This compound ferries long-chain fatty acids into a cell's mitochondria to be burned for energy and is naturally concentrated in muscles like the heart — what is it?
Carnitine: Compound active in mitochondria. Carnitine is a quaternary ammonium compound involved in metabolism in most mammals, plants, and some bacteria.
In calculus, this formula computes the derivative of a composite function by multiplying together the derivatives of its two component functions — what is it called?

Native to Sri Lanka, the inner bark of this evergreen tree is the original source of a beloved baking spice, sometimes distinguished from a cheaper cousin as the 'true' or 'Ceylon' variety — which tree?
Cinnamomum verum: Species of tree. The inner bark of the tree is historically regarded as the spice cinnamon, though this term was later generalized to include C. cassia as well.
Also known as foremilk or historically as 'beestings,' this early substance produced by mammary glands right after birth delivers antibodies and immune factors to newborns. What is it?
Colostrum: Form of milk produced immediately following the delivery of newborn.
First described in 1880 by a French neurologist, this rare delusion convinces sufferers that they are dead, don't exist, or have lost their internal organs — what is it called?
Cotard's syndrome: Delusion that one is dead or non-existent.
Bred in Germany with short legs and a long body to chase badgers into their burrows, which hound breed comes in smooth-, wire-, and long-haired varieties?

Historically defined by having two embryonic seed leaves, this once-standard division of flowering plants covers around 200,000 species but turned out not to share one common ancestor — which plant group?
Dicotyledon: Historical grouping of flowering plants.
This first section of the small intestine, often the principal site of iron absorption, connects the stomach to the middle portion of the intestine — what is it?
Duodenum: First section of the small intestine. The duodenum is the first section of the small intestine in most vertebrates, including mammals, reptiles, and birds.
A Swedish scientist and inventor until, at 53, dreams and visions sent him into a spiritual phase, this polymath became best known for his 1758 book on the afterlife, Heaven and Hell — who was he?
Emanuel Swedenborg: Swedish scientist, philosopher, and theologian (1688–1772)
With a sweet smell like pear drops, this colorless solvent turns up in nail-polish remover and is used to decaffeinate tea and coffee. What is it?
Named after a 19th-century English physicist, this SI unit measures a material's ability to store electrical charge, equal to one coulomb per volt — what is it?
Farad: SI unit of electric capacitance.
Patented in 1962 and sold under a brand name synonymous with 'roofies,' this benzodiazepine is notoriously linked to date-rape drug use — what is it?
Flunitrazepam: Benzodiazepine sedative. Flunitrazepam, sold under the brand name Rohypnol among others, is a benzodiazepine used to treat severe insomnia and assist with anesthesia.
Born in Pisa in 1564, this Italian polymath has been crowned the father of observational astronomy and the scientific method — and was among the earliest tinkerers to build a thermoscope. Who is he?
Galileo Galilei: Italian physicist and astronomer (1564–1642)

This Italian friar and cosmological theorist proposed that stars were distant suns with their own planets, and was tried for heresy by the Roman Inquisition for insisting the universe is infinite — who was he?
Giordano Bruno: Italian Dominican friar, philosopher and mathematician (1548–1600)
Unlike its rocky, mountain-dwelling marmot relatives, this solitary lowland rodent — also called the woodchuck — is common across the Eastern U.S., Canada, and Alaska. What is it?
Groundhog: Species of rodent. The groundhog (Marmota monax), also known as the woodchuck, is a rodent of the family Sciuridae, belonging to the group of large ground squirrels known as marmots.

Often defined as the normal functioning of the body free of disease, pain, or injury, this multidimensional state of well-being can be promoted by exercise and sleep and harmed by smoking or stress — what's the one-word concept?
Health: Desirable level of functional or metabolic efficiency of a living being.
Named for the English physician who first described it in 1832, this cancer is defined by multinucleated Reed–Sternberg cells in the lymph nodes — what is it?
Hodgkin lymphoma: Type of blood and immune-system cancer.
This immune response causes tissue damage upon repeated exposure to an antigen and underlies conditions like hay fever, which affects roughly one in ten people worldwide — what is it called?
Hypersensitivity: Overreaction of the immune system to an antigen.
More than half of all animal species belong to this one chitinous-shelled group, each member sporting three body parts and three pairs of jointed legs — who are they?
Known as sampaguita in the Philippines, where it's the national flower, this fragrant vine or shrub also lends its blossoms to a beloved variety of tea — which species?
Jasminum sambac: Species of jasmine. Jasminum sambac (Arabian jasmine or Sambac jasmine or Mogra) is a species of jasmine native to Bhutan and India.
Also nicknamed the reed or swamp feline, this solitary wild predator ranges from the Caucasus to Southeast Asia and marks territory by urine spraying — which species?

Nicknamed 'acid' and 'Lucy' and derived from the ergot fungus, this semisynthetic hallucinogen is so potent that 20 micrograms produces noticeable effects — yet no fatal human overdose has ever been documented — what is it?
Traditionally kept as an indoor watchdog, this small non-sporting dog breed hails from Tibet — which breed?
Lhasa Apso: Tibetan breed of dog. The Lhasa Apso ( LAH-sə AP-soh) is a non-sporting dog breed originating in Tibet.
This Berkeley professor gave us "fuzzy" everything — fuzzy sets, fuzzy logic, fuzzy control — proposing a whole branch of mathematics for reasoning with imprecision. Who was he?
Defined by milk-producing glands, hair or fur, a broad neocortex, and three tiny middle-ear bones, this animal class split from reptile-and-bird ancestors over 300 million years ago — what is it?
Mammal: Class of animals with milk-producing glands.
Home to the heart, esophagus, trachea, thymus, and central chest lymph nodes, this compartment of the thoracic cavity sits between the lungs — what's it called?
Mediastinum: Central part of the thoracic cavity. The mediastinum (from Medieval Latin: mediastinus, lit. 'midway';pl.: mediastina) is the central compartment of the thoracic cavity.
Grouped by their small size and use of echolocation, this suborder of flying mammals turns out to be genetically distinct from its bigger, fruit-eating relatives — which creatures?

Étienne Geoffroy split these simians into 'Old World' Catarrhini and 'New World' Platyrrhini groups, and counting them without the apes leaves a famously incomplete family tree — what common-name animal is this?
Monkey: Animal of the "higher primates", excluding apes.
Native to southern Europe and North Africa, this fragrant evergreen shrub has berries that are macerated in alcohol to make Mirto liqueur — which plant?
Myrtus communis: Species of flowering plant.
Present in 26 African countries with one of its largest undisturbed populations at Kenya's Lake Turkana, which large crocodilian sees adult males reach 3.5 to 5 metres long?
This British engineer rewrote Maxwell's equations into the form we use today and devised the telegrapher's equations — who was he?
Oliver Heaviside: British mathematician and electrical engineer (1850–1925)
Discovered in 1802 and named after a newly found asteroid, this silvery-white platinum-group metal is prized for cleaning up automobile exhaust in catalytic converters — which element?
Palladium: Chemical element with atomic number 46 (Pd)

Caused by a lack of vitamin B3 (niacin), this disease is remembered for its grim quartet of symptoms — inflamed skin, diarrhea, dementia, and mouth sores — striking sun-exposed skin first. What is it?
Pellagra: Human disease caused by a lack of vitamin B3. The two main types of pellagra are primary and secondary.
With the formula H3PO4, this colorless, odorless compound is typically sold as an 85% aqueous solution and serves as a key ingredient in many fertilizers — what is it?
This plant process moves pollen from an anther to a stigma, eventually letting a tube grow down the style to reach the ovary and enable fertilization. What is it?
Pollination: Biological process occurring in plants.
Encompassing peaches, cherries, plums, and almonds, this genus of flowering trees and shrubs in the rose family produces stone fruits called drupes — which genus?
Prunus: Genus of trees and shrubs.
Botanically a kin of spinach rather than a true grass, this protein-rich Andean pseudocereal was first cultivated near Lake Titicaca thousands of years ago — what is it?
Quinoa: Edible plant in the family Amaranthaceae.
Typically striking two to four weeks after a strep throat, this inflammatory disease can attack the heart, joints, skin and brain — and may permanently scar the heart valves. What is it?
Known as rue or 'herb-of-grace,' this Mediterranean plant is prized for its bluish leaves and doubles as an insect repellent — which species?
Ruta graveolens: Species of plant. Ruta graveolens, commonly known as rue, common rue, ruda, arruda or herb-of-grace, is a species of the genus Ruta grown as an ornamental plant and herb.
Usually forming an S- or C-shaped curve with a rotational twist, this sideways irregular curvature of the spine sits alongside kyphosis and lordosis among the spine's abnormal curves. What is it?
Scoliosis: Left-right asymmetry of the spine's curvature.

This medical condition of inadequate blood flow to body tissues comes in four flavors — hypovolemic, cardiogenic, obstructive, and distributive — and can progress to confusion or cardiac arrest if untreated — what is it called?
Shock (circulatory): Medical condition of insufficient blood flow. Shock is the state of insufficient blood flow to the tissues of the body as a result of problems with the circulatory system.

Self-taught from her father's library and writing to Gauss and Lagrange under a male pseudonym, this French mathematician pioneered elasticity theory and laid groundwork for Fermat's Last Theorem — who was she?
Sophie Germain: French mathematician, physicist, and philosopher.

Striking about one in a million people, this rare neurological disorder brings progressive muscular rigidity and spasms that twist the trunk into postural deformities — first described in 1956, what is it?
Stiff-person syndrome: Neurological disorder. The stiffness primarily affects the truncal muscles and is characterised by spasms, resulting in postural deformities.
Its explosive yield became the standard yardstick for comparing bombs and even asteroid impacts; chemists also use it to make charge-transfer salts — what's this nitro compound?
Discovered via its telltale green spectral line in 1861, this silvery post-transition metal takes its name from the Greek word for a green shoot — which element?
Thallium: Chemical element with atomic number 81 (Tl)
Covered in taste buds and divided into oral and pharyngeal parts, this muscular mouth organ also helps clean the teeth and enable speech — what is it?
Tongue: Muscular organ in the mouth of most vertebrates.
Nicknamed the "immortal jellyfish," this tiny sea creature can revert from a sexually mature adult back into an immature, sea-floor-dwelling polyp stage instead of dying — what species is it?
Turritopsis dohrnii: Species of small, biologically immortal jellyfish.
Commonly called the guelder-rose, this Old World flowering shrub belongs to the Viburnaceae family — what's its scientific name?
Viburnum opulus: Species of flowering plant.
This form of hypertext publication is collaboratively edited and managed by its own audience, working directly through what?
A wiki is a form of hypertext publication on the internet which is collaboratively edited and managed by its audience directly through a web browser.

Born in New York City, this Irish statesman commanded Volunteers at Boland's Mill during the 1916 Easter Rising, narrowly avoided execution due to his American citizenship, and later authored the 1937 Constitution — who is he?
The symbol for copper is Cu. Copper is a chemical element; it has symbol Cu and atomic number 29.

In what year was Winona Ryder born?
Winona Ryder: Winona Laura Horowitz ( wi-NOH-nə; born October 29, 1971), known professionally as Winona Ryder, is an American actress.
In what year was Kendall Jenner born?
Kendall Jenner: Kendall Nicole Jenner (born November 3, 1995) is an American model, socialite and media personality.
In what year was Tommy Lee Jones born?
Tommy Lee Jones: Thomas Lee Jones (born September 15, 1946) is an American actor, film director, and former football player.
In what year was Val Kilmer born?
Val Kilmer: Val Edward Kilmer (December 31, 1959 – April 1, 2025) was an American actor.
In what year was Michelle Yeoh born?
Michelle Yeoh Choo Kheng (YOH;; Chinese: 楊紫瓊; born 6 August 1962) is a Malaysian actress.
In what year was Ian McShane born?
Ian McShane: Ian David McShane (born 29 September 1942) is an English actor.
In what year was Lana Rhoades born?
Lana Rhoades is an American internet personality, podcaster and former pornographic film actress.
In what year was Gwyneth Paltrow born?
Gwyneth Paltrow: Gwyneth Kate Paltrow ( PAL-troh; born September 27, 1972) is an American actress and businesswoman.
In what year was Antonio Banderas born?
Antonio Banderas: José Antonio Domínguez Bandera (born 10 August 1960), known professionally as Antonio Banderas, is a Spanish actor.
In what year was Whoopi Goldberg born?
Whoopi Goldberg: Caryn Elaine Johnson (born November 13, 1955), known professionally as Whoopi Goldberg, is an American actor, comedian, author, and television personality.
In what year was James Gunn born?
James Gunn: James Francis Gunn Jr. (born August 5, 1966) is an American filmmaker.
In what year did Judy Garland die?
Judy Garland (born Frances Ethel Gumm; June 10, 1922 – June 22, 1969) was an American actress, singer, and vaudevillian whose career spanned four decades.
In what year did Paul Newman die?
Paul Newman: Paul Leonard Newman (January 26, 1925 – September 26, 2008) was an American actor, filmmaker, racecar driver, philanthropist, and entrepreneur.
In what year was House of Gucci first released?
House of Gucci: Scott wanted to make a film about the Gucci dynasty after acquiring rights to Forden's book in the early 2000s.
In what year was A Few Good Men first released?
